Fat gain and loss is a function of the amount of glucose in the blood. When it is high, and the muscle is full of glycogen because it was not depleted due to exercise, the muscle does not want more (insulin insensitivity), glucose starts to build in up the blood. Because that is super bad for blood vessels, your body has no other choice than to convert it to fatty acids in the liver and store it as fat.

Similarly, when exercise makes muscles use up their glycogen reserves, they want to load the mup so they become sensitive to insulin. If whatever is coming from food being digested is not enough, the liver converts fatty acids back into glucose and fat gets used up.

And this process is not 1:1 a function of the total amount of calories consumed and burned.

Theoretically, if someone nibbles on refined carbs all day, keeps blood sugar high, and does not exercise, even a relatively low caloric intake can lead to this.

How is that thermodynamically possible? Now, I am not a doctor and could not look it up but I think the idea is basically all other parts of the body will be devoid of nutrition. For example the brain, so I think this can lead to stupidity and so on.

Conversely, that is why low-carb diets work, especially combined with intensive exercise like lifting or sprinting, one can afford to go into a caloric surplus (not extremely of course) without gaining fat. The idea is that blood glucose levels are kept low, partially because exercise makes muscles suck glucose out of the blood like a Hoover partially because meat and vegs just cannot be converted fast enough into glucose to have it really build up in the liver. This means the liver does not transform glucose into fatty acids, it has no reason to, and thus even at a caloric surplus you do not gain fat. What happens with the surplus, then? I think you simply shit it out. Especially that vigorous exercise can make food go through you as much as 50% faster.

So people gain fat not as much because they were eating 300kcal more than they need that day, but at some or multiple points their blood glucose levels were so high that their liver had no choice but to convert it to fat and store it. And at no point at that was it so low that it would convert it back, which, of course, relates to the total calories consumed, constant overeating all the time or overeating on carbs will of course cause that. But if one steak and salad meal was just too big? It will be shat out, as long as the glucose does not shoot up the liver has no reasons to store fat.

This is why low carb is not just a trick to make people consume less calories.

People tend to say low carb diets are high fat diets. Eventually, yes, but it should be understood as lots of meat, not butterhuffing. Raw lard and suchlike is, I fear, too quickly convertable to glucose. A steak, even if nicely marbled, not. So while in the total math a low carb diet is high fat, it is normally not based on "fat looking things" like butter, lard, grease, but rather meat and cheese, the kinds of things we think of as "protein".

What Tim Ferris is saying about slow carbs (lentils, not bread) is also probably true, slow digestion means does not spike the glucose.

This is also why the intermittent fasting stuff works and how Martin Berkhan looks so lean. He eats from 16 o'clock to 24 and does not eat for the next 16 hours. What happens? After 16 hours of fasting, a lot of fat was converted into glucose, and if one lifts as heavy as he does it is a lot of glucose. However 16 hours are not enough for the body to start cannibalizing muscle. Then he puts away an immense amount of meat and his body begins building muscle. Because steak and vegs are not digested too quickly, the blood glucose does not get spiked, besides the muscles are taking it up nicely.
